title: Adaptation: how living things come to fit their homes
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers NCERT Class 5 'Some Unique Places' (ecological regions of India, unique landscapes, rare and endemic species, traditional knowledge) and Cambridge Stage 5 Unit 6.3 'Plants and animals are adapted to different environments' and Unit 6.4 'Adaptations of predators and prey'. No textbook needed.
summary: A camel's feet fit the sand, but nobody shaped them. Your child plays a camouflage game that shows how natural selection works over generations. They meet Alfred Russel Wallace, the self-taught collector who found the idea at the same time as Charles Darwin. They visit India's unique places. In the Western Ghats of Kerala, the purple frog lives underground and has cousins only in the Seychelles. They also visit the Sundarbans, the islands and the Northeast. They test what salt water does to a plant and why hunters have forward-facing eyes. They study how predators and prey shape each other, and find that prey animals of different kinds also help each other. Last, they ask who really 'discovers' an animal that local people already knew.
builds_on: Class 1: every place is somebody's home. Class 2: habitats, and bodies that fit them (cactus, lotus, camel, fish). Class 3: one tree and its soil, shared by day animals and night animals. Class 4: India's landforms. A desert is about water, not heat, and people adapt by culture and even by genes. Next: the Evolution topic follows the whole tree of life, and Living in Harmony follows food webs and living things that depend on each other.
goals: By the end your child can explain what an adaptation is, and how natural selection shapes adaptations over many generations.
By the end your child can tell an adaptation (inherited, over generations) from acclimatisation (changes in one lifetime).
By the end your child can name four of India's unique ecological regions and an endemic species from each.
By the end your child can explain why islands and isolated mountains have so many endemic species, and how drifting continents left the purple frog's cousins in the Seychelles.
By the end your child can list adaptations of predators and of prey, including camouflage, countershading, warning colours and mimicry, and describe the arms race between them.
By the end your child can give examples of cooperation among animals and of local people's knowledge of unique places.
words: adaptation
an inherited feature of body or behaviour that helps a living thing survive and have young in its habitat
natural selection
the process by which living things with helpful features survive and have more young, so those features become common over many generations
variation
the small differences between individuals of the same kind
acclimatisation
a change in one living thing's body during its own life, like getting used to thin air
endemic
found naturally in only one place on Earth
biodiversity hotspot
a region with a great many endemic species that is also under threat
predator
an animal that hunts and eats other animals
prey
an animal that is hunted and eaten
camouflage
colours or shapes that help an animal blend in with its surroundings
countershading
being darker on top and paler underneath, which makes a body look flat and hard to see
mimicry
when one living thing looks like another, to be left alone or to fool others
Gondwana
a giant southern landmass that broke up long ago into Africa, South America, Antarctica, Australia, India, Madagascar and the Seychelles
subconcepts: adaptation: inherited features that help survival and having young
natural selection: variation, inheritance and survival over generations
every adaptation is a trade-off: 'fit for here', not 'best'
India's ecological regions: Western Ghats, Himalaya, Northeast, Sundarbans, islands, Thar
endemic species, and why islands and isolated hills have so many
drifting continents and Gondwana: the purple frog's Seychelles cousins
predator adaptations: forward eyes, speed, stealth, pack hunting
prey adaptations: side eyes, camouflage, armour, herds, alarm calls
cooperation between species: langurs and chital
local and traditional knowledge of unique places

days.title: The camouflage game: how bodies come to fit
days.goal: Recall last year's landforms and see natural selection happen in a game.

steps.title: Lands and lives recall
steps.do: Ask: 'Last year we travelled across India. Why is Ladakh a desert?' (very little rain or snow, not heat.) 'How are a camel, a yak and a person in Jaisalmer each adapted?' Then ask the big question for this year: 'A camel's feet fit the sand perfectly. But who made them fit? Did the camel try? Did someone design it?' Let your child give any answer and write it down. You'll come back to it.

steps.title: Hungry birds, hidden insects
steps.do: Do Activity a1, the selection game. Cut 40 small squares from newspaper and 40 the same size from plain coloured paper. These are 'insects'. Scatter 20 of each on a big spread of newspaper, and keep the rest as a spare pile. Your child is a hungry bird. They pick up insects one at a time, as fast as they can, until they have eaten 20. Count how many of each kind are left. The survivors 'have babies': for each insect left, add one more of the same kind from the spare pile. Play three or four 'generations' and write the numbers in a table. Ask: 'What happened to the coloured insects? Did any insect TRY to become newspaper-coloured?'

steps.title: The three ingredients
steps.do: Explain the idea using the game. 1) Variation: insects were not all the same. 2) Inheritance: babies look like their parents. 3) Selection: the ones that were harder to see survived and had more babies. Repeat for many, many generations and the whole group comes to fit its background. That is natural selection, and the features it builds are adaptations. Nobody planned it, and no insect tried. Go back to the camel's feet: 'How could natural selection explain them?' (Long ago, camels with slightly wider feet sank less, survived better and had more young.)

steps.title: One sentence
steps.do: Your child finishes two sentences: 'An adaptation is…' and 'It comes from…' (An inherited feature that helps a living thing survive and have young. It comes from natural selection over many generations.) Ask: 'Is a person who gets a tan in summer adapting?' Keep the answer for Day 2.

need: plain coloured paper (red, yellow or blue)

days.title: Two men, one idea, and the trade-off
days.goal: Meet Wallace and Darwin, and see that adaptation is about fitting a place, not being the best.

steps.title: A fever in the Spice Islands
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v1: Alfred Russel Wallace, a poor, self-taught collector, lost four years of specimens when his ship burned and sank, and still went back out to the Malay islands. In 1858, ill with fever in the Malay islands, he worked out natural selection and posted his essay to Charles Darwin, who had been quietly working on the same idea for 20 years. Ask the voice question. Ask: 'Why do you think almost everyone knows Darwin's name, and fewer know Wallace's?'

steps.title: Adapting or getting used to it?
steps.do: Go back to yesterday's tan question. Explain: a tan, getting used to thin air in Ladakh, or stronger legs from cycling are changes in one body during one life. This is called acclimatisation. It is not passed to your children. An adaptation is inherited and built over many generations, like the EPAS1 gene of Tibetan people from Class 4. Sort five examples together. A camel's wide feet: adaptation. A trekker breathing faster in Leh: acclimatisation. A yak's long hair: adaptation. A dog growing a thicker coat in winter: acclimatisation, though being able to grow it is an adaptation. A cactus's spines: adaptation.

steps.title: Drama: the perfect animal
steps.do: Your child plays a 'perfect' animal that boasts it can live anywhere: 'I have the camel's feet, the polar bear's fur, the fish's gills and the cheetah's legs!' You play the habitats one by one. Desert: 'Your fur is cooking you!' Sea: 'Your camel feet can't swim!' Snow: 'Your gills froze!' Help your child see that every adaptation costs something: fur is heavy and hot, speed burns energy, big brains need lots of food. Then ask: 'Is a cheetah better than a tortoise? Better at what? Where?' (A cheetah can sprint for less than a minute. Some tortoises live more than 100 years.)

steps.title: Trade-off list
steps.do: Make a two-column list: 'Adaptation' and 'What it costs'. Fill five rows together. A cheetah's speed: they tire within a minute, and often lose their kill to lions and hyenas. A tortoise's shell: safe from bites, but heavy and slow. A chital's side eyes: a wide view all round, but poor at judging distance in front. A polar bear's thick fur: they overheat when they run. Our big brain: it uses about a fifth of our body's energy. Ask: 'Is there any adaptation with no cost?'

days.title: The Western Ghats and the underground frog
days.goal: Meet India's unique places and endemic species, and see how drifting continents shaped them.

steps.title: Story: The Frog Who Lives Below
steps.do: Read the story 'The Frog Who Lives Below' aloud. Don't explain it. Ask the story questions, especially: 'Why does the frog say her cousins are across the sea?' and 'Who knew about the frog before the scientists?'

steps.title: Biju, Bossuyt and the 'underworld frog'
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v2. In 2003 S.D. Biju and Franky Bossuyt described the purple frog to science. They showed that this frog is so different from all other frogs that they needed a new family, with their closest cousins in the Seychelles islands. Local people in Kerala already knew the frog. They called them 'pathala thavala', Malayalam for 'underworld frog'. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: The Gondwana jigsaw
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Print or trace a world map. Cut out Africa, South America, India, Madagascar, Australia, Antarctica and the Seychelles (draw them as a dot if they are too small). Your child tries to fit them together like a jigsaw into one big land, Gondwana. Then move India slowly north and away, leaving Madagascar and the Seychelles behind, until it bumps into Asia (and pushes up the Himalaya, from Class 4). Ask: 'If a family of frogs lived on the land that became India and the Seychelles, what happens to them when the land splits?' (They are separated. Each group changes in their own way for tens of millions of years.)

steps.title: Endemic and hotspot
steps.do: Explain: a species found naturally in only one place is endemic. The Western Ghats are full of them: the lion-tailed macaque, the Nilgiri tahr, the purple frog, Malabar gliding frogs, many fish, birds and plants found nowhere else. Islands and isolated mountain tops have many endemics, because animals and plants there are cut off and change in their own way. A place with very many endemic species that is also under threat is called a biodiversity hotspot. India has parts of four: the Himalaya, the Indo-Burma region in the Northeast, the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (the Nicobar Islands). Ask: 'Why would losing a forest in a hotspot be worse than losing one elsewhere?' (Their species may live nowhere else. Once they are gone from there, they are gone from the whole Earth.)

days.title: Salt forests, islands and root bridges
days.goal: Travel to the Sundarbans, the islands and the Northeast, and test how salt water challenges plants.

steps.title: Salt water and a plant
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Put a cucumber slice and a carrot stick in plain water, and the same in very salty water. Ask: 'Mangroves grow in salty mud by the sea. What do you think salty water will do to these pieces of plant? Why?' Check after 30 minutes and again tomorrow.

steps.title: The Sundarbans
steps.do: Ask: 'What problems would a tree have in salty mud that the sea covers twice a day?' (The salt, and mud with no air in it for the roots.) Then explain how mangroves cope. Some of their roots stick up out of the mud like snorkels, to breathe. These roots are called pneumatophores. Some kinds push extra salt out through their leaves, and some store it in old leaves that they then drop. Their seeds sprout while still on the tree, then drop and float to new mud. India has mangroves at Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu, Bhitarkanika in Odisha and, biggest of all, the Sundarbans, which India shares with Bangladesh. The Sundarbans are the largest mangrove forest in the world. Tigers there swim between islands. Fishing cats, river dolphins, crabs and mudskippers live there too. Ask: 'How is a Sundarbans tiger's life different from the life of a tiger in the dry forest of Bandipur?' (They swim a lot and live with salty mud and tides.)

steps.title: Islands and the Northeast
steps.do: Islands: the Andaman and Nicobar Islands have endemics like the Narcondam hornbill, found only on one small island, and the Nicobar megapode, a bird that buries their eggs in mounds of sand and rotting leaves and lets the heat hatch them. The Northeast: India's only ape, the hoolock gibbon, swinging and singing in the treetops, and the sangai deer of Manipur's Loktak Lake, which lives on floating mats of plants. And people: the Khasi and Jaintia people of Meghalaya guide the living roots of rubber fig trees across streams for years until they become living bridges that grow stronger with age. Ask: 'Is a living root bridge a human adaptation, a tree's, or both?'

steps.title: Root bridge challenge
steps.do: Using string, wool or pipe cleaners and two stacks of books as the stream banks, your child weaves a 'root bridge' that can hold a small toy. Rule: no tape, only twisting and weaving, as the Khasi do with roots. Ask afterwards: 'Why would a living bridge get stronger with time, when a wooden one rots?'

steps.title: Map pins
steps.do: Add the Western Ghats, Pichavaram, the Sundarbans, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Meghalaya and Manipur to your map from Class 4, with one endemic or special species for each.

need: last year's map or a printed map of India

days.title: The hunters
days.goal: Find out how predators are adapted, with your own eyes as the test.

steps.title: Check the salt test
steps.do: Look at Experiment e1 together. Ask: 'Which pieces are floppy? Which are crisp?' (The ones in salt water are floppy. The ones in plain water are crisp.) Explain: water moves out of the plant towards the salty side. Mangroves face this problem every day, and their adaptations deal with it.

steps.title: One eye or two?
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Your child closes one eye and tries to touch the tips of two pencils together, or put a cap on a pen held at arm's length. Then with both eyes. Then stand still and, looking straight ahead, see how far round to the side they can see a wiggling finger. Ask: 'Why do owls, cats, tigers and we have eyes facing forward? Why do chital, rabbits and pigeons have eyes on the sides?'

steps.title: Hunters' tool kits
steps.do: Ask: 'What is a hunter's problem?' (Prey hide, watch and run away.) Then go through predator adaptations, and ask your child how each one helps. Tiger: stripes break up their outline in tall grass, padded paws are silent, and they ambush from close range. Cheetah: long legs, a bendy spine and claws that grip the ground like running spikes, for short bursts of great speed. Owl: forward eyes for judging distance, soft-edged feathers for silent flight, and, in barn owls, ears at different heights that find a mouse by sound. Kingfisher: watches from a perch, then dives beak-first. Dhole (Indian wild dog), found in forests like Bandipur and Nagarhole in Karnataka: they hunt in whistling, cooperating packs that can bring down a sambar many times their size. Spider: builds a web, a trap, instead of chasing. Ask: 'Which hunter here works as a team?'

steps.title: Silent owl walk
steps.do: Play 'owl and mouse' in a dim room: your child, blindfolded, is the owl in the middle and must point to where the 'mouse' (you) is, using only sound, as you move slowly and crinkle a piece of paper. Then swap: the owl must stay totally silent while 'flying' across the room on tiptoe, arms out, to tag the mouse. Ask: 'Which was harder, hunting by sound or moving silently? Real owls do both.'

steps.title: Hunter card
steps.do: Your child chooses one Indian predator and makes a 'hunter card': a drawing and three adaptations, each with how it helps. Ask: 'What does this predator's adaptation cost them?' (See the Day 2 list.)

need: two pencils or a pen and its cap
a piece of paper to crinkle

days.title: The hunted: hide, warn, fool or flee
days.goal: Discover the many ways prey survive, and test countershading.

steps.title: The shadow trick
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. Make two tubes from grey card. Leave one plain. Shade the other darker on top and lighter underneath. Put both on a table under a ceiling light or in sunlight, and step back three metres. First ask: 'Which one do you think will be harder to see?' Then look and ask: 'Which one looks round and solid? Which looks flat?' Explain that many fish, deer, birds and caterpillars are darker on top and paler underneath. This is called countershading.

steps.title: Thayer's right idea and his wrong one
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v3, Abbott Thayer, the painter who worked out countershading and was right, and then said ALL animal colours, even flamingos' pink, were camouflage, and was wrong. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: The prey tool kit
steps.do: Ask: 'What is a prey animal's problem?' (Hunters are watching for them.) Then go through prey adaptations. Hiding: the stick insect, the Indian oakleaf butterfly (bright on top, dead-leaf brown underneath), the nightjar on the forest floor. Warning: bright colours that say 'I taste horrible' or 'I sting', as on the plain tiger butterfly and many beetles. Mimicry: harmless animals that look like the warning ones. Some tasty butterflies look like bad-tasting ones. Henry Walter Bates noticed this in the Amazon in 1862. Armour: the tortoise, and the pangolin, who rolls into a ball of scales. Fleeing: side eyes for watching all round, and long legs. Togetherness: herds and flocks have many eyes and ears. Ask: 'Which would you choose to be, a hider, a warner, a fooler or a runner?'

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1. For the 'why' questions, ask your child to use one of the new words in each answer (adaptation, natural selection, camouflage, endemic).

need: 2 sheets of grey card or paper

days.title: The arms race, and the alliance
days.goal: See how hunters and hunted shape each other, and how prey species help each other.

steps.title: The arms race
steps.do: Explain: as prey get faster, only the faster predators catch enough to survive and have young. As predators get sharper-eyed, only the best-hidden prey survive. Each side shapes the other over generations, like an arms race. Example: bats hunt moths by echolocation, finding them by the echoes of their calls. Some moths evolved ears that hear bat calls, and they dive when a bat comes near. Some tiger moths click back, which jams the bat's echolocation. Ask: 'Does an arms race ever end?' (Not while both sides exist.)

steps.title: Why does the zebra have stripes?
steps.do: Talk about voice v4: scientists argued for over a century about zebra stripes. Ask your child for their guess first. Then give the evidence: Tim Caro and colleagues found striped animals live where biting flies are worst, and that flies fail to land on horses wearing striped coats. Other ideas: confusing lions, keeping cool, recognising friends. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: The langur and the chital
steps.do: Tell your child about a real alliance in Indian forests, from Nagarhole in Karnataka to Kanha in Madhya Pradesh. Langur monkeys sit high in trees, and chital (spotted deer) graze below. Langurs can see far, and they give loud alarm calls when they spot a tiger or leopard. Chital hear the langur alarms and run. Chital have a keen sense of smell and give their own alarms, and langurs respond to those too. Langurs also drop fruit and leaves that the chital eat. Ask: 'Is this competition or cooperation? Who gains?' Then: 'Is survival only about being the strongest?'

steps.title: Paint a hidden creature
steps.do: Take a photo of a surface near your home and print it, or draw it carefully: a wall, a tree trunk, a patch of grass, a tiled floor. Your child invents a creature camouflaged to live exactly there, and paints it right into the picture so it is hard to find. Show it to someone in the family and time how long they take to spot it. Ask: 'Would your creature still be hidden somewhere else in the house?'

steps.title: Hunt or Hide card game
steps.do: Play the card game g1: predators play a hunting tactic and prey must answer with a defence that beats it, explaining why.

need: a printed photo or a careful drawing of a surface at home

days.title: Who knows a place? Protecting what is unique
days.goal: Weigh local and scientific knowledge, finish the project and teach it back.

steps.title: Who knows a forest?
steps.do: Talk through the perspectives in this pack: the Soliga people of the Biligiri Rangaswamy hills, the Khasi root-bridge builders, the Kerala families who knew the purple frog long before 2003. Ask: 'When a scientist "discovers" a frog that local people already knew, who discovered it?' Then: 'What can a scientist add that local people may not have, and what do local people know that a scientist may not?' (Scientists can compare animals across the world, read their DNA and publish. Local people know the seasons, habits and uses of living things, and how they have changed over generations.)

steps.title: Unique place project
steps.do: Finish the project: your child presents their poster of one unique place in India: where it is, its climate and landform, three endemic or special species with one adaptation each, the local people and what they know, and one threat and one way it is being protected. Ask: 'If you could make one rule to protect this place, what would it be, and who would you ask first?'

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2. Talk through each written answer before your child writes it.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child teaches the whole topic back to the family using the camouflage game results, the Gondwana jigsaw and their hunter card: what an adaptation is, how natural selection works, why the Western Ghats have endemic frogs with Seychelles cousins, how predators and prey shape each other, and how prey cooperate. Go back to their Day 1 answer about who made the camel's feet fit, and ask if they would change it. Ask the check questions. For deeper thinking, do Worksheet ws3 another day.

need: the camouflage game table and Gondwana jigsaw

opts: they tried hard to change colour
the bird found them harder to see, so more survived and had young

Match the species to its unique place.
The purple frog's closest relatives live in the Seychelles because…
opts: India and the Seychelles were once joined, then drifted apart

rolling into a ball of scales

A caterpillar is green on top and pale underneath. This is…
A harmless butterfly looks almost exactly like a bad-tasting one. This is…

Match the attack to the defence that evolved against it.

sections.p: Imagine the birds in our camouflage game learned to search slowly and carefully. What would happen to the insects over many generations?

sections.p: Some people say evolution means 'survival of the fittest', so the strongest always win. Using the langurs and chital, the dhole pack and the trade-offs you found, argue whether that is the whole story.
The purple frog was known to people in Kerala for generations, but scientists 'discovered' the frog in 2003. Write what a fair story of this discovery would say.
Humans live in almost every kind of place on Earth. Is that because our bodies are adapted to all of them, or because of clothes, houses and fire? Give an example of each.
Design an experiment to test whether countershading really hides an animal from a predator. What would you measure?

experiments.title: Salt water and a plant
experiments.question: What does salty water do to a plant?
steps: Fill both glasses with the same amount of water.
Stir 4 tablespoons of salt into one glass until mostly dissolved.
Put one cucumber slice and one carrot stick in each glass.
After 30 minutes, take them out and bend them gently. Compare.
Look again the next day.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which will stay crisp and which will go floppy? Why?'
experiments.observe: The pieces in salt water go soft and floppy and may shrink. The pieces in plain water stay crisp or get crisper.
experiments.why: Water moves through the walls of plant cells from where there is less salt to where there is more (osmosis). In salty water, water is pulled out of the plant's cells, so they collapse and the plant wilts, even though they are sitting in water. That is why salty soil kills most plants. Mangroves have adaptations that most plants lack: some keep salt out at their roots, some push it out through glands on their leaves, and some store it in old leaves that they drop.
experiments.safety: Don't eat the salty pieces. Wash hands after.

experiments.title: One eye or two?
experiments.question: Why do hunters and hunted have their eyes in different places?
need: two pencils, or a pen and its cap
steps: Hold a pencil in each hand at arm's length. Close one eye and try to bring the tips together. Try 5 times and count successes.
Do it again with both eyes open.
Now look straight ahead without moving your eyes. Your partner stands behind you and slowly brings a wiggling finger round from behind, on one side. Say 'now' when you first see it.
Look at pictures of an owl, a tiger, a chital, a rabbit and a pigeon. Where are their eyes?
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will one eye be just as good as two for touching the tips?'
experiments.observe: With one eye it is much harder to judge distance. You can see a wiggling finger quite far to the side, but not behind you.
experiments.why: When two eyes face forward, they see the same scene from slightly different places, and the brain uses the difference to judge distance very precisely. Predators like owls, cats and eagles need this to pounce. Prey animals like chital, rabbits and pigeons have eyes on the sides of their heads, which gives them a much wider view, almost all the way round, to spot danger, but less ability to judge distance in front. It is a trade-off. Humans, apes and monkeys also have forward-facing eyes, which help them judge distance when they reach and grab.
experiments.safety: Hold pencils gently and away from faces.

experiments.title: The shadow trick: countershading
experiments.question: Does being darker on top and lighter underneath help an animal hide?
need: 2 sheets of grey card or paper
a light from above (ceiling light or sunlight)
steps: Roll both sheets into tubes the same size and tape them.
Leave one tube plain grey.
On the other, shade the top half darker and leave the bottom paler, blending smoothly from top to bottom.
Lay both on their sides on a grey or brown surface with light shining from above.
Step back about 3 metres and squint. Which looks round? Which looks flatter? Ask someone else too.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which tube will be harder to see?'
experiments.observe: The plain tube looks round and solid, because light from above makes its top bright and its underside shadowy. The shaded tube looks flatter and blends in better.
experiments.why: Light from the sky makes the top of any body bright and its belly dark, and that pattern tells a predator's eye 'here is a solid, round thing'. Countershading cancels it out: a darker back and paler belly make the body look evenly coloured and flat, so it melts into its background. Many fish, deer, birds and caterpillars are countershaded. The painter Abbott Thayer described this in the 1890s, and it is sometimes called Thayer's law.

activities.title: Hungry birds, hidden insects: the selection game
need: several sheets of newspaper spread out
40 the same size cut from plain coloured paper
steps: Scatter 20 newspaper 'insects' and 20 coloured ones over the newspaper. Keep the rest as a spare pile.
The 'bird' picks up insects one at a time, as fast as they can, until 20 have been eaten.
Count how many of each kind were eaten and how many are left.
For each survivor, add one more of the same kind from the spare pile (they have babies). There are 40 insects again.
Repeat for 3 or 4 generations, writing down the numbers each time.
Draw a simple bar chart for each generation.
activities.outcome: A table and chart showing camouflaged insects becoming more common over generations, without any insect trying to change: natural selection in action.

activities.title: The Gondwana jigsaw
need: a big sheet of paper and glue
steps: Cut out Africa, South America, Antarctica, Australia, India, Madagascar and the Seychelles.
Fit them together into one southern supercontinent, Gondwana (India sits beside Madagascar and Antarctica).
Draw a frog family on the India-Seychelles join.
Slowly slide India north, leaving Madagascar and the Seychelles behind, until it meets Asia.
Glue the final positions on the sheet and draw arrows showing India's journey.
activities.outcome: A map showing how drifting continents separated the purple frog from their Seychelles cousins.

project.title: A unique place of India
steps: Choose one unique place: the Western Ghats, the Sundarbans, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Meghalaya's forests, Loktak Lake, the Thar, or the high Himalaya.
Find its landform and climate.
Find three endemic or special species, and one adaptation of each.
Find out about the people who live there and one thing they know about it.
Find one threat and one way it is being protected.
Make a poster and present it on Day 8.
project.outcome: A poster about one of India's unique places, its adapted life and its people.

game.title: Hunt or Hide
rules: Cut out the cards. Make a HUNTER pile (12 cards) and a HIDER pile (12 cards). One player takes each pile and draws 4 cards.
The hunter plays one card face up: a predator and its tactic.
The hider must play a defence card that would beat that tactic and say WHY in one sentence. If the other player agrees, the hider wins the round and keeps both cards.
If the hider has no card that works, the hunter keeps both. Both players draw back up to 4.
Swap roles halfway. The player with the most cards when the piles run out wins.
Bonus: if a hider plays 'Langur alarm call' or 'Herd of many eyes', they win any round against an ambush.

cards.front: HUNTER: tiger, ambush from tall grass
HUNTER: eagle, sharp eyes from high up
HUNTER: snake, smells with their tongue
HUNTER: crocodile, waits at the water's edge
HUNTER: shikra, a small hawk that bursts out of a tree
HIDER: stick insect, looks like a twig
HIDER: tiger moth, clicks to jam sonar
HIDER: chital, side eyes and quick start
HIDER: pangolin, rolls into a ball of scales
HIDER: plain tiger butterfly, tastes horrible
HIDER: frog that freezes and stays still

big: If nobody designed the camel's feet, how did they come to fit the sand so well?
Is any living thing 'better' than another, or only better at something, somewhere?
Who discovers a frog: the scientist who names it, or the people who always knew it?
Is survival about being the strongest, or about fitting in and getting along?
Humans have changed every habitat. Are we still being shaped by places, or only shaping them?
If a place is unique, who does it belong to?

challenge.q: 'Survival of the fittest' means the strongest, fiercest animals win. Is that what Darwin and Wallace meant?
challenge.hint: 'Fittest' means best fitted to a place, like a key fits a lock, not strongest. The phrase was coined by Herbert Spencer, and Darwin adopted it later. A well-hidden stick insect, a cooperating pack of dholes, and chital listening to langurs are all 'fit'. Cooperation, hiding and patience win as often as strength.

challenge.q: We often hear that animals adapt because they need to, as if a giraffe stretched its neck and its babies were born with longer necks. True?
challenge.hint: That was Jean-Baptiste Lamarck's idea, about 200 years ago. Evidence went against it: changes in one body during life are generally not passed on through genes. Natural selection works on differences that are already there. Scientists are still studying 'epigenetics', ways some effects of a parent's life can reach the next generation, but it does not work like the giraffe story.

challenge.q: The purple frog was 'discovered' in 2003. Was it?
challenge.hint: It was described to science in 2003 by S.D. Biju and Franky Bossuyt. People in the Western Ghats had seen it for generations, especially when it came up in the monsoon, and had their own name for it. Science added something real: the frog's family tree and their link to the Seychelles. Who should share the credit?

perspectives.who: The Soliga people of the Biligiri Rangaswamy hills, Karnataka
perspectives.view: The Soliga have lived in these forests for centuries, gathering honey, gooseberries and lichens, and using controlled cool fires. When the area became a tiger reserve, they won the legal right to stay and keep their ways. Some ecologists argue that forests where local people are partners are protected better than forests emptied of people. Others worry that too much may be harvested. Ask: should people be part of a protected forest, or kept out of it?

perspectives.who: The Khasi root-bridge builders of Meghalaya
perspectives.view: A living root bridge takes many years, often more than ten, to grow strong enough to cross. The person who starts one is often building it for their grandchildren. Ask: what would you start today that only someone else would finish?

I can't climb trees. The langurs can't smell a tiger as well as I can. So I listen to them and they listen to me, and we both live. Ask: if a deer and a monkey can be allies, why do we tell stories of nature as only a battle?

My family has lived under these hills since before there were Himalaya. Your scientists described us in 2003. Ask: what other beings might be living quietly under our feet, unknown to science but not unknown to themselves?

voices.who: Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913), Britain, with Charles Darwin (1809–1882)
voices.idea: Wallace came from a poor family, left school at 14 and taught himself natural history. He paid for his expeditions by collecting and selling specimens. In 1852 his ship home from the Amazon caught fire and sank with almost all his collections. He went out again, to the Malay Archipelago, and in 1858, ill with fever on the island of Ternate, he worked out natural selection and posted his essay to Darwin. He also noticed a sharp invisible line between islands with Asian animals and islands with Australian ones, now called the Wallace Line, and became a founder of biogeography, the study of where living things live and why.
voices.then: Darwin, who had been working on the same idea privately for about 20 years, was shocked. Their two papers were read together at the Linnean Society in London in July 1858, while Wallace was still far away and was not asked first. Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859 and became far more famous. Wallace was generous about it all his life, and even called his own book on the idea 'Darwinism'.
voices.now: Natural selection is accepted as a central mechanism of evolution, with a mountain of evidence. Historians agree Wallace discovered it independently, and that his poverty, his distance from London and his lack of powerful friends are part of why he is less remembered.
voices.ask: Two people found the same idea, one rich and well connected in England, one poor and feverish on an island. What makes one name become famous? What evidence would you look at to decide who deserves credit?

voices.who: S.D. Biju, India, and Franky Bossuyt, Belgium (2003), and the people of the Western Ghats
voices.idea: In 2003, Biju and Bossuyt described the purple frog, Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis, from the Western Ghats in Kerala. This frog spends most of the year deep underground, feeding on termites with a pointed snout and a grooved tongue, and comes up for only a few weeks in the monsoon to breed in streams. Their DNA showed that they belong to their own ancient family, whose closest living relatives are tiny frogs in the Seychelles islands, separated from India when the old southern continent broke apart tens of millions of years ago.
voices.then: The discovery was published in Nature and astonished scientists: a large, ancient lineage had been overlooked by science in one of the world's most studied countries. Local people, however, had long known the frog. They saw them in the rains and called them pathala thavala, Malayalam for 'underworld frog'.
voices.now: Accepted. The purple frog is now a symbol of the Western Ghats' unique life and of how much remains unknown there. Biju has gone on to describe dozens of new frog species from India. Many are threatened as forests are cleared and streams dammed.
voices.ask: Science added the frog's family tree and their link to the Seychelles. Local people knew where and when to find it. How could the two kinds of knowledge be put together, fairly?

voices.idea: Thayer, a painter, noticed that many animals are darker on top and lighter underneath, and showed with models that this 'countershading' makes a round body look flat and hard to see under light from the sky. This is still called Thayer's law. He then went much further, claiming in a 1909 book with his son Gerald that almost ALL animal colouring is camouflage, including the bright pink of flamingos (to match sunrise and sunset skies) and the peacock's shimmering tail.
voices.then: His countershading idea was widely admired and later influenced how warships were camouflaged. His bigger claim was mocked, most famously by Theodore Roosevelt, a keen naturalist, who pointed out that many bright animals are plainly showing off, not hiding.
voices.now: Countershading is accepted. The claim that all colour is camouflage is rejected: many colours are for attracting mates, warning predators or signalling to others. A flamingo's pink comes from pigments in the algae and shrimp they eat. Thayer was brilliantly right about one thing and wrong about where to stop.
voices.ask: Thayer was right about countershading and wrong about flamingos. How can a scientist tell when a good idea is being stretched too far?

voices.who: Tim Caro and colleagues (from 2014), USA and UK: why do zebras have stripes?
voices.idea: For more than a century people argued about zebra stripes: do they confuse lions, keep zebras cool, help them recognise each other, or something else? In 2014 Caro's team compared where striped animals live and found the strongest link was with biting flies, which spread disease. In 2019 they put horses in striped coats and filmed flies: the flies slowed down near the stripes and failed to land properly.
voices.then: Supporters of the other ideas pointed out that a link on a map is not proof, and that stripes might do more than one job at once.
voices.now: The biting-fly idea has the most evidence so far, but scientists still argue about whether it is the only reason, and exactly how stripes confuse a fly's eyes.
voices.ask: If you wanted to test whether stripes confuse lions, what experiment could you do without harming any zebra?

story.title: The Frog Who Lives Below
text: I live underneath. Underneath the tea gardens and the cardamom and the wet red earth of the hills that your maps call the Western Ghats, three metres down, where it is dark and close and smells of roots. I have lived here all my life, and so did my mother, and so did hers, back and back, further than there are numbers for.

I am fat and purple-grey, the colour of a rain cloud at evening. My eyes are small, because there is nothing to look at down here. My nose is a hard little point, like the tip of a spade, and my arms are short and strong, made for pushing through soil. I swim through the earth the way a fish swims through water, slowly, with my nose in front. When I am hungry, I find a tunnel of the termites, and I slide my long grooved tongue into it, and I eat. That is most of what I do, for most of the year. It is a quiet life. I like it.
But once a year, the earth speaks to me.

It begins with a smell. Far above, the first heavy rains of the monsoon are falling, and the water soaks down, down, through the leaves and the roots and the soil, and reaches me as a cold, sweet trickle along my back. Then I know. I turn my pointed nose upward and I begin to dig.

It takes many nights. When I come out, it is like being born. The air is huge and wild and loud. The stream beside me is roaring. The rain is drumming on every leaf. There are other voices, the voices of my own kind, calling from the stream banks: a deep, soft call, like a hen clucking from inside a jar. I add my own.
That year, there was also a light.

It came bobbing along the stream bank in the dark: a torch, held by a young man in a soaked shirt, with a girl of about ten beside him holding an umbrella that was doing no good at all. The light stopped on me. I froze. Freezing is what we do.
"There," whispered the girl. "I told you. That's the one."
The young man crouched. He was very still for a long time. When he spoke, his voice had changed.
"I have never seen anything like it," he said. "Not in any book. Not in any museum. What do you call it?"
The girl shrugged, as if it were a silly question. "My grandmother calls them the frog from below. They come up when the big rains come, every year. Then they go back down."
"Every year," said the young man softly. "And nobody wrote it down."
"We didn't need to write it down," said the girl. "We knew."

The young man looked at the girl then, and I think something passed between them, though I cannot read faces. Then he gently lifted me, measured me, looked very closely at my nose and my strong short arms, and took a tiny piece of skin from my toe, which hardly hurt, and put me back exactly where I had been, by the roaring stream.
I did not know what he did with that tiny piece of me. But I know now, because the story has come back to the hills, the way stories do.

He found the long chain of letters inside it, the recipe every living thing carries. And he found that I am not like the other frogs of these hills. I am not like the frogs of anywhere in India, or Asia, or the world. My closest cousins, the scientists said, are tiny frogs that live on a handful of islands in the middle of the ocean, far to the west, called the Seychelles.
How could that be? I have never seen the sea.

Here is what I have come to understand, lying in the dark through the long dry months, thinking slowly, the way we do. Long, long ago, before the Himalaya were pushed up, before there were tigers or elephants or people, the land above me was joined to other lands, all in one great country. My ancestors lived there, in the wet earth, digging and eating and coming up once a year in the rain. Then the land began to split, very slowly, as slowly as I dig. One piece drifted west and became small islands. Our piece drifted north for millions of years, carrying us on its back like a great raft, until it bumped into Asia.

My cousins were carried one way, and we were carried the other. They became small and quick and lived in the leaf litter. We became fat and pointed and learned to swim through soil. We have not met for longer than you can imagine. And still, inside us both, the same old recipe remembers that once we were one family.
The scientists gave me a long name and a family of my own. They put my picture in famous journals. People came from far away to see me.

But the girl's grandmother still calls me the frog from below. She knew me first. And every year, when the earth speaks to me and I dig up into the roaring dark, it is the children of her village who come with their torches and umbrellas, laughing, to say: there, there, they've come back.
Then the rains ease, and I turn my nose down again, and go home.
story.epiphany: Adaptation and deep time: the purple frog's body (pointed snout, short strong arms, small eyes, termite tongue) fits a life underground, built by natural selection over tens of millions of years. Its closest relatives are in the Seychelles because the land that became India and the Seychelles were once joined in Gondwana and drifted apart, carrying separated relatives that then adapted in different ways. This is why isolated places have endemic species. The turn is the frog realising 'once we were one family' across the ocean. Underneath: who 'discovers' something, when local people already knew it. Based on the real purple frog described by S.D. Biju and Franky Bossuyt in 2003. The scene at the stream is imagined.
ask: How is the frog's body suited to living underground?
Why does the frog say her closest cousins are across the sea?
Who knew about the frog first? Who 'discovered' it?
What did the girl mean by 'We didn't need to write it down. We knew'?
If the frog and her Seychelles cousins met today, would they recognise each other?

ideas.idea: Nobody designed the fit: natural selection did.
ideas.more: Variation, inheritance and survival, repeated over many generations, shape bodies to their places. The camouflage game shows it in minutes. Nature does it over thousands and millions of years.

ideas.idea: Every adaptation has a cost, and fits one place, not every place.
ideas.more: Speed, fur, armour and big brains all cost something. A cheetah is not better than a tortoise. Each one fits their own way of living.

ideas.idea: Continents move, and they carried living things apart.
ideas.more: Drifting continents separated families of frogs, and isolated places grow their own endemic species. The purple frog of Kerala and the frogs of the Seychelles are cousins on separated rafts of land.

ideas.idea: Animals help each other as well as compete.
ideas.more: Predators and prey shape each other. But chital listen to langurs, dholes hunt as a team and babblers watch together. 'Fittest' means best suited to a place, not strongest.

unknowns: How many species in the Western Ghats and the Northeast are still unknown to science? New frogs, fish and plants are described almost every year, and nobody knows how many are left to find.
Why exactly do zebra stripes stop flies landing, and is that their only job? Scientists are still testing it.
Can unique species like the purple frog and the Narcondam hornbill adapt fast enough as the climate warms and forests shrink? Nobody knows.
How much of animal colour is camouflage, how much is warning and how much is for attracting mates? For many animals, scientists still don't know.

books.title: On the Origin of Species
books.author: Sabina Radeva (a picture-book retelling of Charles Darwin's book)
books.why: Darwin's great argument told in clear words and beautiful pictures: variation, selection, deep time and the tree of life.

books.title: Grandmother Fish: A Child's First Book of Evolution
books.author: Jonathan Tweet
books.why: Very simple and warm: we got our wiggles from fish and our grip from apes. A good bridge for younger siblings too.

books.title: One Day in the Tropical Rain Forest
books.author: Jean Craighead George
books.why: A boy races to find a new species before a forest is cut down, hour by hour through one day of rainforest life.

books.title: The Song of the Dodo
books.author: David Quammen
books.age: adult (read the chapters on Wallace in the Malay islands aloud)
books.why: Why islands have so many unique species and why they vanish so easily, with the full story of Wallace.

check.q: What is an adaptation? Give one example from India.
check.a: An inherited feature that helps a living thing survive and have young where it lives. For example: the mangrove's breathing roots, the purple frog's spade-like snout, the snow leopard's thick fur and long tail.

check.q: Explain natural selection with the three ingredients.
check.a: Individuals vary. Young inherit features from their parents. Those with helpful features survive and have more young, so over many generations those features become common.

check.q: What is the difference between adaptation and acclimatisation?
check.a: An adaptation is inherited and builds up over generations. Acclimatisation is a change in one body during their own life, like a tan or getting used to thin air, and it is not passed on.

check.q: Why does the purple frog have cousins in the Seychelles?
check.a: India and the Seychelles were once joined in Gondwana. When the land split and drifted apart, the frog families were separated, and each changed in their own way.

check.q: What does endemic mean, and why do islands have many endemic species?
check.a: Found naturally in only one place. On islands and isolated hills, living things are cut off and change in their own way over time.

check.q: Give two predator adaptations and two prey adaptations.
check.a: Predators: forward-facing eyes, silent feathers, speed, pack hunting, webs. Prey: side eyes, camouflage, countershading, warning colours, mimicry, armour, herds, alarm calls.

check.q: Give an example of cooperation between two species.
check.a: Langurs and chital warn each other of tigers and leopards, and langurs drop food for chital.
A self-taught British naturalist who discovered natural selection independently of Darwin in 1858, while ill on the island of Ternate, and founded the study of where species live.
